\subsection{Further questions and research}\label{smc:xi:sec:further}
\wtag\ The merge raised two questions of its own. They are recorded here instead of being asserted or dropped.
\begin{enumerate}
\item\label{smc:xi:q:gates} \emph{Can source~30's two acceptance gates be merged?} Source~29's single outer equation (O13) also excludes the time-zero match of a rotation: at exponent $0$ its Gaussian data are $P=1$, $C=1$, $S=0$. Source~30 uses two gates, (O13) for time zero and (O14) for positive times, and notes that for a general elliptic map the times zero and one both have denominator one (Section~\ref{smc:pl:sec:extraction}). A merged gate would bring source~30's ledger to $80J$ witnesses and $43J$ equations, matching source~29's per-contact count. Argument sketch: choose the companion basis $S=[z,A^{-1}z]$ so that the time-zero point $e_1$ is the image of the exponent $m=-1$ of the same coefficient recurrence. Missing: a positive-domain encoding of that shifted exponent within one POWER pair, and a proof that the extraction bound of Section~\ref{smc:pl:sec:extraction} still separates the two candidates. Neither source claims that such a merge is possible.
\item\label{smc:xi:q:bridge} \emph{A uniform clock family.} Source~27 needs two machines for its two clock behaviours, a 138-event Zeno word and a separately reclosed 114-event non-Zeno variant (Theorem~\ref{smc:fv:thm:clock}). Source~32's 44-event word has both behaviours (Theorem~\ref{smc:pj:thm:mixed}), because its return matrix has the unit mode that the invariant $c=D-3y/2$ detects. Does every rational fixed-centre lift with a unit eigenvalue and a contracting complement admit one word that is Zeno on the contracting face and non-Zeno inside? Missing: a general invariant, which source~32 has only for its example, and control of the exact one-word chamber along the face.
\end{enumerate}

Both carry the author line ``Research report'' and name no assistant; their recorded run logs show the runtime of an AI pipeline. Neither names a ProveIt commit, path or gap. Source~35 pins source~34, and together they pin sources~28, 30 and~33 and the mathlib Pell source by SHA-256; and every pin resolves to a shipped file or to a file of the arrival archive (the README lists them). Their labels carry the prefixes \texttt{smc:br:} and \texttt{smc:ck:}; their equations are numbered within this report's sections, and where the pipeline's report numbers appear in their text, the bracketed source numbers after them were added in the merge.

\wtag\ \textbf{What the two sources do.} Source~34 builds, for every fixed deterministic two-counter program, one finite rational-speed signal machine with number-preserving (cardinality-preserving) binary rules and exactly five live signals---four stationary markers and one messenger---that simulates the program from every initial counter pair on one fixed ordered full section $L<X<Y<R$. Its devices are an exact \emph{nondestructive} branch test, whose two complete words have the exact open chambers $4x<y<8x$ and $8x<y$ and are undone by a physically implemented, branch-tagged inverse, and a powers-of-two encoding that every guard covers uniformly. It adds, independently of the physics, a quartic with a unique positive witness for halting within a fixed instruction horizon. Source~35 pads every instruction of that compiler to exactly $30D$ (at most 54 contacts, one common set of 39 speeds), and replaces the externally supplied exponential initialization by three native positive integer gaps (still of numeric height $\Theta(2^m)$) whose decoding it pays for inside two displayed 15-residual POWER modules: joint degree~12, $T(E+2)+54$ positive witnesses at horizon~$T$, a unique decoded trace, and infinite full witness fibres. It also computes the exact primitive integer initialization and its bit height.

\wtag\ \textbf{What is not new.} Counter computation with five live signals is Durand-Lose's MCU 2004/2005 construction~\cite{dl2004mcu} (two fixed scale signals, two counter-position signals and one instruction signal, with cardinality-preserving rules), which both sources credit prominently. Part~XII is therefore \emph{not} a new universality result and not a minimum-population result; neither source claims either. What the sources add is the fixed ordered full-section interface with literal label restoration, the exact nondestructive branching, the uniform guard coverage, the exact clock and the costed native-gap certificate. Opposite-speed reversal is standard~\cite{DL06}, and bouncing delays are an established mechanism, used explicitly by Durand-Lose and Emmanuel~\cite{dle2021agc11}. No universal counter program is constructed, so no universal machine with an explicit table is printed here.

\noindent{\large\bfseries Source 34 (batch-91 manuscript 16): Nondestructive branching with five live signals}\par
\noindent\emph{A uniform counter compiler on one fixed ordered section}, ``Research Report 64'', 4 October 2026. \wtag\ From the archive \path{Five_signal_branching_source_and_evidence.zip}, main file \path{Report64/Report64.tex} (a byte-exact flattening of the eleven modules in its \path{manuscript/}). Its labels carry the prefix \texttt{smc:br:}; its sections are Sections~\ref{smc:br:sec:main}--\ref{smc:br:sec:evidence} here, its Appendix~A being printed as Section~\ref{smc:br:sec:evidence}; its table of contents and page breaks are omitted. Its two branch labels, which it wrote \texttt{\textbackslash ZZ} and \texttt{\textbackslash NN}, are written $\brZ$ and $\brN$ here (sans serif, as in the source): $\brZ$ marks the zero branch and $\brN$ the nonzero branch, and neither is the set $\Z$ or $\NN$. Its natural numbers include~$0$ and are written~$\NN$. Its diagram colours carry the prefix \texttt{smcbr}. Its bibliography is merged into the report's.
\begin{quote}\small
We construct a finite physical test that returns four stationary markers and one messenger to exactly the same ordered section while retaining one of two branch labels. The two complete collision words have exact open chambers $4x<y<8x$ and $8x<y$ inside $0<x<y<D$; their nondestructive versions use 14 and 12 events. A separated powers-of-two encoding makes these guards valid for every nonnegative pair of counters. Explicit increment and positive-decrement gadgets then give one finite rational-speed rule table per fixed finite two-counter program, independent of its initial counters. Exactly five signals remain live, every nonhalting instruction has at most 32 binary events and duration $D<T<10D$, and all instruction sections restore the same marker ordering, labels, scale and messenger speed. Infinite encoded computations have no finite-time collision accumulation. A companion finite-trace construction gives a unique positive-integer witness for each fixed instruction horizon: one quartic equation with $T(E+2)$ witnesses and $T(E+Z+4)+1$ residuals before bundling, where $E$ counts split edges including a virtual halt loop and $Z$ counts zero edges. Its arity grows with the horizon. Five-live-signal counter computation already appears in Durand-Lose's MCU 2004/2005 work; the result here is the fixed full-section interface, exact nondestructive branching and uniform guard coverage, not a new universality or minimum-population claim.
\end{quote}
\section{Main result and scope}\label{smc:br:sec:main}
A \emph{meta-signal} is a finite label with a fixed rational speed. A \emph{live signal} is an individual occurrence of such a label. Our count of five concerns live signals, not the number of labels or speeds. At an outgoing section the five strands are
\begin{equation}\label{smc:br:eq:section}
 L=0,\qquad X=x,\qquad Y=y,\qquad R=D,\qquad Q\text{ at }L\text{ outgoing at }+1,
 \qquad 0<x<y<D.
\end{equation}
The four marker labels have speed zero. The messenger and $L$ are counted as two outgoing strands at their common section contact. All later contacts on the encoded executions are binary, have distinct incoming and distinct outgoing speeds, and are separated by positive time. Deterministic collision rules consume and produce the same number of signals.

\begin{theorem}[Uniform fixed-program compiler]\label{smc:br:thm:compiler}
For every fixed finite deterministic two-counter program consisting of increment, zero-test/positive-decrement, and halt instructions, there is an effectively specified finite rational-speed collision table that simulates that program for every initial pair $(a,b)\in\NN^2$ on the single section \eqref{smc:br:eq:section}. The encoding is
\begin{equation}\label{smc:br:eq:encoding}
 x=D\left(\frac1{20}+\frac1{10}2^{-a}\right),\qquad
 y=D\left(\frac{19}{20}-\frac1{10}2^{-b}\right),\qquad D>0.
\end{equation}
Every nonhalting simulated transition restores the four stationary marker labels, the scale $D$, and the speed-$+1$ outgoing messenger, whose control label identifies the next instruction. It uses at most 32 binary collisions and has duration strictly between $D$ and $10D$. The rule table uses only the 19 rational speeds in \eqref{smc:br:eq:speeds}. Exactly five signals remain live, and an infinite encoded computation has no finite-time collision accumulation.
\end{theorem}

The finite table depends on the \emph{fixed program}, not on $a$, $b$, $D$, or the number of executed instructions. A separately chosen fixed universal counter program would give one table through this compiler. That conditional corollary is different from saying that every counter program runs on one table without an interpreter or program encoding. No particular universal counter program is constructed here. \wtag\ [Compare Part~III, which writes out one fixed reversible universal table with 18 live signals (Theorem~\ref{smc:cs:thm:literal}). A universal counter program compiled by Theorem~\ref{smc:br:thm:compiler} would give one five-signal table that is number preserving but not claimed reversible; none is written out in this report.]

\begin{theorem}[Nondestructive full-section test]\label{smc:br:thm:test}
On either of the full-dimensional open chambers
\begin{align}
 \PZ&=\{(D,x,y):x>0,\ y-4x>0,\ 8x-y>0,\ D-y>0\},\label{smc:br:eq:PZ}\\
 \PN&=\{(D,x,y):x>0,\ y-8x>0,\ D-y>0\},\label{smc:br:eq:PN}
\end{align}
a finite rule table returns exactly the same $(D,x,y)$ and stationary marker labels, while outputting distinct messenger phases $Q_{\mathrm{out},\brZ}$ and $Q_{\mathrm{out},\brN}$. It uses respectively 14 and 12 events. Branch acquisition is a real choice of local collision partners. No marker-only collision changes a remote messenger label.
\end{theorem}

\subsection{Historical boundary of the claim}
Durand-Lose's MCU 2004/2005 construction already encodes two counters by two position signals, uses two fixed scale signals and one instruction signal, and preserves signal cardinality \cite{dl2004mcu}. The five-live-signal computational precedent is therefore prior work. There the counter markers can exchange order, and a zero counter lies beyond the unit marker. This report supplies a different certified interface: every instruction begins and ends in the fixed order $L<X<Y<R$, with literal label restoration and one scale. Its specific additions are the two exact branching chambers, a nondestructive test and guard coverage for the entire encoded state set. No novelty, priority, minimum-population or exhaustive-literature claim is made.

The preceding local-realization proof (retained with the evidence) establishes physical map gadgets around suitable points. Local existence alone does not imply a single encoding covered by every future instruction guard, nor does it implement a branch. Those are precisely the issues treated here. The argument below is self-contained for the test and the update primitives used by the compiler. \wtag\ [The local-realization proof is source~33's (Part~XI, Theorem~\ref{smc:hl:thm:main}); the copy that source~34 retained is shipped once, as \path{33-homogeneous-science-frozen-proof-PROOF.md}.]
\section{An explicit changing test}\label{smc:br:sec:branch}
We first permit $X$ to change position. Section~\ref{smc:br:sec:inverse} undoes that change physically while preserving the outcome in finite labels. Only $L$, $X$, $Y$ and the messenger participate; $R$ is a stationary spectator.

\subsection{Labels, speeds and local rules}\wtag\ [$\brZ$ and $\brN$ are finite branch tags (zero and nonzero tested counter), not the sets $\Z$ and~$\NN$. The messenger labels $C_{\brZ},C_{\brN}$ are unrelated to the conditional-state count~$C$ and the control residuals $C_t$ of Section~\ref{smc:br:sec:certificate}.]\par
The stationary target label is $X_0$. Its moving labels and speeds are
\[
 X_{\mathrm{pre}}:-\frac12,\qquad X_{\mathrm{fast}}:+2,\qquad X_{\mathrm{post}}:-\frac12.
\]
The messenger labels are distinct, including those with equal speeds:
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrrrrr}
\text{label}&Q_0&Q_1&Q_2&Q_3&Q_4&C_{\brZ}&C_{\brN}\\\hline
\text{speed}&1&-3/2&1&-1/4&4&-1&-1
\end{array}
\]
The rules preceding the final anchor contact are
\begin{align}
 \{Q_0,X_0\}&\ruleto\{Q_1,X_{\mathrm{pre}}\},\label{smc:br:eq:forwardrules}\\
 \{Q_1,L\}&\ruleto\{Q_2,L\},\nonumber\\
 \{Q_2,X_{\mathrm{pre}}\}&\ruleto\{Q_3,X_{\mathrm{fast}}\},\nonumber\\
 \{Q_3,L\}&\ruleto\{Q_4,L\},\nonumber\\
 \{X_{\mathrm{fast}},Y\}&\ruleto\{X_{\mathrm{post}},Y\},\nonumber\\
 \{Q_4,X_{\mathrm{post}}\}&\ruleto\{C_{\brZ},X_0\},\nonumber\\
 \{Q_4,X_{\mathrm{fast}}\}&\ruleto\{C_{\brN},X_0\}.\nonumber
\end{align}
At $L$, each $C_c$ emits a distinct speed-$+1$ phase. In the nondestructive gadget this is the reverse-entry phase in Section~\ref{smc:br:sec:inverse}; the anchor contact is a single interface event, not two instantaneous events.

The rule with input $\{X_{\mathrm{fast}},Y\}$ changes only those two participants. The branch is learned later, when $Q_4$ meets either $X_{\mathrm{post}}$ or $X_{\mathrm{fast}}$. Thus branch acquisition is local even though its geometric cause is an earlier marker-only contact.

\subsection{The common prefix}
The messenger begins at $L$ with speed $+1$. Table~\ref{smc:br:tab:prefix} specifies all positions needed for the first three events. The other markers stay at $L=0$, $Y=y$, $R=D$.

Event & Time & Messenger & $X$ & Contact\\\midrule
Section & $0$ & $0$ & $x$ & outgoing $L,Q_0$\\
1 & $x$ & $x$ & $x$ & $Q_0,X_0$\\
2 & $5x/3$ & $0$ & $2x/3$ & $Q_1,L$\\
3 & $19x/9$ & $4x/9$ & $4x/9$ & $Q_2,X_{\mathrm{pre}}$\\\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Common prefix of the two changing-test words. The initial section is not counted as a new event.}\label{smc:br:tab:prefix}

After event 3, the messenger travels left at $-1/4$ and $X$ right at $+2$. The messenger reaches $L$ at
\begin{equation}\label{smc:br:eq:AB}
 B=\frac{35x}{9};\qquad
 A=\frac{17x}{9}+\frac y2
\end{equation}
is the prospective time at which this fast $X$ reaches $Y$. Since
\[
 A-B=\frac{y-4x}{2},
\]
both selected chambers have the anchor bounce first. At $B$, the target is at $4x$ and the messenger acquires speed $+4$. If the target were to remain fast, they would meet at time $53x/9$ and position $8x$. Consequently $y<8x$ gives the $X/Y$ contact first, whereas $y>8x$ gives the messenger/fast-target contact first. This comparison is made only after the common prefix and anchor bounce are valid.

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{The $\brZ$ word: $4x<y<8x$}{The Z word: 4x<y<8x}}
Set
\begin{equation}\label{smc:br:eq:F}
 F=\frac{10y-8x}{9}.
\end{equation}
The word continues as in Table~\ref{smc:br:tab:Z}. Its seven positive flight durations are
\begin{equation}\label{smc:br:eq:Zdurations}

 \frac{y-4x}{2},\quad\frac{2(8x-y)}{9},\quad F.
\end{equation}
The return map is $(D,x,y)\mapsto(D,F,y)$. Its determinant is $-8/9$, as expected for the odd-length seven-event word; this determinant is a consistency check, not a substitute for chronology. \wtag\ [The sign $(-1)^7$ is the parity rule of source~31 (Theorem~\ref{smc:iv:thm:parity}); the six-event $\brN$ word below has determinant $+8$ accordingly.]

\section{Complete chronology and exact chambers}\label{smc:br:sec:chronology}
\subsection{Why the endpoint checks suffice}
Throughout either changing-test word, the strands have weak spatial order
\[
 L,\ Q,\ X,\ Y,\ R,
\]
with exactly the indicated adjacent contact at an event and every other gap strictly positive. This is an order of live strands, not of finite phase labels. At common events 1--3 the positive target positions $x$, $2x/3$, $4x/9$ lie below $y$; at event 4, $X=4x<y$.

At the marker-only $\brZ$ event 5,
\[
 0<2y-8x<y
\]
because $4x<y<8x$. At event 6,
\begin{equation}\label{smc:br:eq:Fgap}
 F>0,\qquad y-F=\frac{8x-y}{9}>0.
\end{equation}
At the final anchor bounce $X=F$ stays strictly between $L$ and $Y$. For $\brN$, the inequality $0<8x<y$ certifies the final two rows. In both cases $R$ stays beyond $Y$.

Every adjacent gap is affine during a flight. If positive at both endpoints it is positive throughout. A departure gap has positive outgoing derivative; an arrival gap has negative incoming derivative. Since collision partners have distinct speeds, a gap zero at just one endpoint is strictly positive in the open flight. Hence no additional adjacent gap can vanish, and a nonadjacent meeting is impossible without an adjacent meeting. Together with \eqref{smc:br:eq:Zdurations} and \eqref{smc:br:eq:Ndurations}, this proves the \emph{complete} collision chronology, including the absence of simultaneous remote contacts.

\subsection{Positive coefficient certificates}
The chamber coordinates make the strict inequalities checkable without numerical samples. On $\PZ$ put
\begin{align}
 \alpha&=y-4x>0,&\beta&=8x-y>0,&\gamma&=D-y>0,\nonumber\\
 x&=(\alpha+\beta)/4,&y&=2\alpha+\beta,&D&=2\alpha+\beta+\gamma.\label{smc:br:eq:Zcoordinates}
\end{align}
On $\PN$ put
\begin{align}
 \alpha&=x>0,&\beta&=y-8x>0,&\gamma&=D-y>0,\nonumber\\
 x&=\alpha,&y&=8\alpha+\beta,&D&=8\alpha+\beta+\gamma.\label{smc:br:eq:Ncoordinates}
\end{align}
Every noncontact event gap and every flight duration is a nonzero linear combination of these three positive quantities with nonnegative rational coefficients. For example, in \eqref{smc:br:eq:Zcoordinates}, the fourth-event target distance is $4x=\alpha+\beta$, the fifth-event messenger distance is $2\alpha$, and
\[
 F=2\alpha+\frac{8\beta}{9},\qquad y-F=\frac{\beta}{9}.
\]
The arithmetic evidence records coefficient rows for every gap, rather than testing a selection of counter values.

\subsection{Necessity and the first forbidden event}
The stated chambers are exact for the two selected complete words. Once the common prefix is valid, having event 4 precede the marker-only contact requires $y>4x$. Having that contact precede the fast messenger catch then requires $y<8x$. Together with the initial ordering these give precisely $\PZ$. The $\brN$ word requires the fast messenger catch before any $X/Y$ contact, hence $y>8x$, giving precisely $\PN$.

At $y=4x$ the messenger/$L$ contact and the $X/Y$ contact are simultaneous at different locations. At $y=8x$ the messenger, $X$ and $Y$ meet together. Both boundaries are excluded. There is a lower post-contact chamber $x<y<4x$ for the underlying machine, but its word is neither claimed as part of this test interface nor needed for the counter encoding. \wtag\ (See item~\ref{smc:xii:q:lowchamber} of Section~\ref{smc:xii:sec:further}.) Necessity is proved at the \emph{first} ordering failure; no invalid trajectory is continued through an earlier wrong event.
\section{The physical inverse and the retained branch}\label{smc:br:sec:inverse}
\subsection{The anchor interface is a real collision}
Negating velocities at an arbitrary outgoing section would be an externally imposed operation. Instead, the last forward anchor collision is used as the phase interface. Its incoming messenger speed is $-1$, so it can emit a reverse-entry messenger at $+1$. The reverse phase first undoes the preceding \emph{non-anchor} event. At the other end, a new $L$ collision emits the desired forward output phase. There is no zero-time duplicate event at either join.

For $c\in\{\brZ,\brN\}$ introduce fresh reverse labels. A bar denotes the negative of the corresponding forward speed, and the subscript $c$ preserves the branch. Stationary base marker labels are retained. In particular $\overline C_c$ has speed $+1$. The final forward anchor rule is
\begin{equation}\label{smc:br:eq:interface}
 \{C_c,L\}\ruleto\{\overline C_c,L\}.
\end{equation}
The two reverse-entry rules are
\begin{align}
 \{\overline C_{\brZ},X_0\}&\ruleto
   \{\overline Q_{4,\brZ},\overline X_{\mathrm{post},\brZ}\},\label{smc:br:eq:reverseentry}\\
 \{\overline C_{\brN},X_0\}&\ruleto
   \{\overline Q_{4,\brN},\overline X_{\mathrm{fast},\brN}\}.\nonumber
\end{align}
The additional marker-only rule for $\brZ$ is
\begin{equation}\label{smc:br:eq:reversemarker}
 \{\overline X_{\mathrm{post},\brZ},Y\}\ruleto
 \{\overline X_{\mathrm{fast},\brZ},Y\}.
\end{equation}
For either branch $c$, use
\begin{align}
 \{\overline Q_{4,c},L\}&\ruleto\{\overline Q_{3,c},L\},\label{smc:br:eq:reverserules}\\
 \{\overline Q_{3,c},\overline X_{\mathrm{fast},c}\}&\ruleto
     \{\overline Q_{2,c},\overline X_{\mathrm{pre},c}\},\nonumber\\
 \{\overline Q_{2,c},L\}&\ruleto\{\overline Q_{1,c},L\},\nonumber\\
 \{\overline Q_{1,c},\overline X_{\mathrm{pre},c}\}&\ruleto
     \{\overline Q_{0,c},X_0\},\nonumber\\
 \{\overline Q_{0,c},L\}&\ruleto\{Q_{\mathrm{out},c},L\}.\nonumber
\end{align}
Both output phases have speed $+1$. They may be different next-instruction labels or entry phases of later blocks. All rules are binary and have distinct outgoing speeds.

\subsection{A literal reflected chronology}
Write the forward event times as
\[
 0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_m=T.
\]
After the outgoing interface at time $T$, the reverse events occur at elapsed times
\begin{equation}\label{smc:br:eq:reversetimes}
 T-t_{m-1},\ T-t_{m-2},\ \ldots,\ T-t_1,\ T.
\end{equation}
These are elapsed \emph{event times}, not successive flight durations. The reverse flights themselves have lengths
\[
 t_m-t_{m-1},\ t_{m-1}-t_{m-2},\ \ldots,\ t_1-t_0.
\]
They are all positive. The first $m-1$ inverse contacts occupy the forward event positions in reverse order. The last is the fresh terminal $L$ bounce. Between contacts the complete five-strand geometry is the forward geometry at the reflected time, with all moving velocities negated. Strict separations are therefore inherited exactly.

At the terminal section, $X$ is again at $x$, $Y$ at $y$, and the anchors at $0,D$. Every stationary marker has its original label. Branch tags remain in the messenger despite the common reverse prefix geometry. The output coordinate map is the identity on all three homogeneous coordinates, with no residual moving marker, shifted scale or hidden marker phase.

The changing word and its inverse use $2m$ events in total: 14 for $\brZ$ and 12 for $\brN$. Their durations are
\begin{equation}\label{smc:br:eq:testtimes}
 T_{\mathrm{test},\brZ}=\frac{25(2x+y)}9,
 \qquad T_{\mathrm{test},\brN}=\frac{250x}{9}.
\end{equation}
This proves Theorem~\ref{smc:br:thm:test}. The method uses the standard opposite-speed reversal principle \cite{DL06}; the explicit boundary rules and branch tags are essential here. It constructs an inverse \emph{gadget} using fresh labels. It does not claim that the entire collision table, after completion on unused inputs, is globally reversible. \wtag\ [Source~31 (Part~XI) draws the same line between the invertibility of a fixed word and global reversibility.]

\section{An encoding covered by every test guard}\label{smc:br:sec:encoding}
Local gadget validity is not enough for a computation: every state reached later must stay in a certified guard. The encoding \eqref{smc:br:eq:encoding} makes this invariant explicit.

\subsection{Two uniformly separated bands}
For every finite nonnegative pair $(a,b)$,
\begin{equation}\label{smc:br:eq:bands}
 \frac D{20}<x\le\frac{3D}{20},\qquad
 \frac{17D}{20}\le y<\frac{19D}{20}.
\end{equation}
Even the closure of this rectangle lies strictly inside $0<x<y<D$. As a counter tends to infinity, its encoding tends to an ordinary interior shape; the limiting section does not merge markers. This does not make the encoding noise robust: resolving unbounded counters still requires arbitrarily fine exact distances.

When $a=0$, $x=3D/20$, so
\begin{equation}\label{smc:br:eq:zero-margins}
 y-4x\ge\frac D4,\qquad 8x-y>\frac D4,\qquad
 x\ge\frac D{20},\qquad D-y>\frac D{20}.
\end{equation}
Every zero-$A$ state lies in $\PZ$, uniformly over $b$. When $a>0$, $x\le D/10$, so
\begin{equation}\label{smc:br:eq:positive-margins}
 y-8x\ge\frac D{20},\qquad x>\frac D{20},\qquad D-y>\frac D{20}.
\end{equation}
Every positive-$A$ state lies in $\PN$. The secondary remote-tie boundary $y=4x$ and the primary branch boundary $y=8x$ are both separated from the encoded inputs. The intermediate changing-test section is also nondegenerate: on the zero branch,
\[
 y-F=\frac{8x-y}{9}>\frac D{36};
\]
on the positive branch, $y-8x\ge D/20$. Hence the physical reverse does not conceal a shrinking gap at its entry section.

\subsection{Testing the other counter by reflection}
Use distance from $R$ as a reflected coordinate. The nearest target and the spectator then have distances
\begin{equation}\label{smc:br:eq:reflection}
 r=D-y=D\left(\frac1{20}+\frac1{10}2^{-b}\right),\qquad
 s=D-x=D\left(\frac{19}{20}-\frac1{10}2^{-a}\right).
\end{equation}
They satisfy exactly the same inequalities as $(x,y)$. Negating all physical speeds and exchanging the left/right roles realizes the same test for $b$. Reflection changes neither flight durations nor distance-coordinate guards.

The transfer from the standard $L$ section to the reflected $R$ section has three contacts: cross $X$, cross $Y$, bounce at $R$. It takes time $D$. The return transfer crosses $Y$, crosses $X$, then bounces at $L$, also taking three events and time $D$. Transfer crossing rules preserve the marker and use fresh messenger phases. Their endpoint bounce selects the next block's entry phase. All six crossings and bounces are counted; none is a remote relabeling.

Thus one encoding simultaneously covers every $A$ and $B$ test, independently of counter magnitudes. No finite-cover argument is inferred from local realization, and no initial counter value is used to choose a different compiled table.
\section{Explicit uniformly guarded counter updates}\label{smc:br:sec:updates}
Use distance coordinates from an anchor $A=0$, with a nearest target $M_0$ at $t$, a stationary spectator $S$ at $s$, and a far reflector $B=D$, where $0<t<s<D$. These are roles occupied by the existing four markers; no extra marker is introduced. \wtag\ [In this section $A$ and $B$ name the anchor and the far reflector, not the two counters $A,B$ of Section~\ref{smc:br:sec:compiler}, and $h$ is a speed, not the halt edge of Section~\ref{smc:br:sec:certificate}.] Reflection gives the right-anchor versions.

\subsection{Four-event anchored scaling}
For fixed rational $k>0$, put
\[
 h=\frac{k-1}{k+1},\qquad -1<h<1.
\]
Give the target label $M_h$ speed $h$. Fresh messenger labels $K_0,K_1,K_2,K_3$ have respective speeds $+1,-1,+1,-1$. The complete rule schema is
\begin{align}
 \{K_0,M_0\}&\ruleto\{K_1,M_h\},\label{smc:br:eq:scalerules}\\
 \{K_1,A\}&\ruleto\{K_2,A\},\nonumber\\
 \{K_2,M_h\}&\ruleto\{K_3,M_0\},\nonumber\\
 \{K_3,A\}&\ruleto\{K_{\mathrm{out}},A\}.\nonumber
\end{align}
Here $K_{\mathrm{out}}$ has speed $+1$. The collision times and positions are
\begin{equation}\label{smc:br:eq:scaletable}
 (t,t),\quad(2t,0),\quad(2t+kt,kt),\quad(2t+2kt,0).
\end{equation}
The target identity is $t+h(t+kt)=kt$. Its moving segment is monotone between $t$ and $kt$. The exact guard is
\begin{equation}\label{smc:br:eq:scaleguard}
 0<t<s<D,\qquad 0<kt<s.
\end{equation}
These endpoint inequalities make every flight positive and exclude every spectator contact. If an endpoint is obstructed, an adjacent contact or a collapsed/reordered flight occurs no later than the proposed restoration. The operation fixes $s,D$, restores the base labels and has duration $2(1+k)t$.

\subsection{Ten-event translation}
For rational $e<1$, the translation $t\mapsto t+eD$ has exact guard
\begin{equation}\label{smc:br:eq:translationguard}
 0<t<s<D,\qquad 0<t+eD<s.
\end{equation}
Put
\begin{equation}\label{smc:br:eq:translationparams}
 u=\frac{t}{1-e},\qquad h=\frac e{2-e}.
\end{equation}
First scale $t$ to $u$ using \eqref{smc:br:eq:scalerules} with $k=1/(1-e)$; this uses target speed $h$. Its final anchor bounce emits $V_0$ at speed $+1$.

For the remaining six-event part, take messenger speeds
\[
 V_0,V_1,V_2:+1,\qquad V_3,V_4,V_5:-1.
\]
Use a fresh moving target label $M'_h$ of speed $h$, with rules
\begin{align}
 \{V_0,M_0\}&\ruleto\{V_1,M'_h\},\label{smc:br:eq:translationrules}\\
 \{V_1,S\}&\ruleto\{V_2,S\},\nonumber\\
 \{V_2,B\}&\ruleto\{V_3,B\},\nonumber\\
 \{V_3,S\}&\ruleto\{V_4,S\},\nonumber\\
 \{V_4,M'_h\}&\ruleto\{V_5,M_0\},\nonumber\\
 \{V_5,A\}&\ruleto\{V_{\mathrm{out}},A\}.\nonumber
\end{align}
The output speed is $+1$. The six messenger positions are
\[
 u,\quad s,\quad D,\quad s,\quad t+eD,\quad0.
\]
The six flight lengths (and times, because the messenger speed has magnitude one) are
\begin{equation}\label{smc:br:eq:translationflights}
 u,\quad s-u,\quad D-s,\quad D-s,\quad s-(t+eD),\quad t+eD.
\end{equation}
The target restoration identity is
\begin{equation}\label{smc:br:eq:translationidentity}
 u+h\bigl[2D-(t+eD)-u\bigr]=t+eD.
\end{equation}
The hidden intermediate position is guarded by the same endpoint inequalities, since
\[
 u-t=\frac{et}{1-e},\qquad
 (t+eD)-u=\frac{e\,[D-(t+eD)]}{1-e}.
\]
Both differences have the sign of $e$, so $u$ lies between $t$ and $t+eD$. The target then stays strictly inside $(0,s)$. Every spectator crossing is explicitly included, and the target cannot meet either anchor. The complete translation takes ten events and duration
\begin{equation}\label{smc:br:eq:translationtime}
 2\left[t+\frac{t}{1-e}\right]+2D.
\end{equation}
This is the needed nearest-target primitive from the retained Report~63 [source~33] proof, with its rules and guard re-established here. \wtag\ [It is source~33's Lemma~\ref{smc:hl:lem:primitive}.] Only the rational values used below enter the final compiler.

\subsection{Increment and positive decrement}
For an encoded distance
\[
 t=\frac D{20}+\frac D{10}2^{-n},
\]
increment $n\mapsto n+1$ is the two-block operation
\begin{equation}\label{smc:br:eq:increment}
 t\ \longmapsto\ \frac t2\ \longmapsto\ \frac t2+\frac D{40}.
\end{equation}
It uses scaling $k=1/2$ and translation $e=1/40$. Since $D/20<t\le3D/20$, its scale endpoint is at most $3D/40$ and its final endpoint belongs to $(D/20,D/10]$. All remain positive and strictly below the spectator distance $s\ge17D/20$.

For $n\ge1$, positive decrement $n\mapsto n-1$ is
\begin{equation}\label{smc:br:eq:decrement}
 t\ \longmapsto\ 2t\ \longmapsto\ 2t-\frac D{20}.
\end{equation}
It uses scaling $k=2$ and translation $e=-1/20$. The positive branch gives $D/20<t\le D/10$. Its scale endpoint is in $(D/10,D/5]$, and its final endpoint in $(D/20,3D/20]$. Again both guards hold uniformly, including the intermediate scale inside the translation. No positive-decrement claim is made for a zero input.

Each update has $4+10=14$ events, preserves the other counter, and restores the full anchor section. The target speeds in distance coordinates are
\begin{equation}\label{smc:br:eq:updatespeeds}
 -\frac13,\quad+\frac13,\quad\frac1{79},\quad-\frac1{41}.
\end{equation}
For clarity, substituting into the block durations yields
\begin{align}
 T_{\mathrm{inc}}&=2D+\frac{196}{39}t,\label{smc:br:eq:updatetimes}\\
 T_{\mathrm{dec}}&=2D+\frac{290}{21}t.\nonumber
\end{align}
The admitted ranges prove $2D<T_{\mathrm{update}}<4D$. For example, the increment coefficient multiplies at most $3D/20$ and the decrement coefficient at most $D/10$. The strict lower bound follows from $t>0$. Reflecting the same blocks updates counter $B$.
\section{One finite table and unbounded computation}\label{smc:br:sec:compiler}
\subsection{The instruction semantics}
The deterministic instruction set is
\begin{align*}
 &\operatorname{INC} A;\ \operatorname{goto}j,\qquad
   \operatorname{INC} B;\ \operatorname{goto}j,\\
 &\text{if }A=0\text{ then goto }j_0\text{, else }A:=A-1\text{ and goto }j_1,\\
 &\text{if }B=0\text{ then goto }j_0\text{, else }B:=B-1\text{ and goto }j_1,\\
 &\operatorname{HALT}.
\end{align*}
An instruction section uses the base stationary labels and messenger $Q_i$ at $L$ outgoing at speed $+1$. The index $i$ is the finite control state. For each instruction and branch make fresh copies of all temporary phases and moving-marker labels needed by its blocks. The copies enlarge the finite alphabet but do not create additional live signals.

An interface is implemented by selecting the outgoing messenger label at the existing final anchor contact of the preceding block. It does not add another event at the same spacetime point. Table~\ref{smc:br:tab:compile} gives the complete block compilation and its event counts.
\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering\small\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.3}
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{.21\linewidth}p{.62\linewidth}r@{}}\toprule
Instruction branch & Physical blocks & Events\\\midrule
$\operatorname{INC} A$ & Left update; final bounce emits $Q_j$ & 14\\
$\operatorname{INC} B$ & Transfer to $R$, reflected update, transfer to $L$ & 20\\
Conditional $A$, zero & Left nondestructive $\brZ$ test; emit $Q_{j_0}$ & 14\\
Conditional $A$, positive & Left $\brN$ test, positive decrement; emit $Q_{j_1}$ & 26\\
Conditional $B$, zero & Transfer to $R$, reflected $\brZ$ test, transfer to $L$ & 20\\
Conditional $B$, positive & Transfer to $R$, reflected $\brN$ test, positive decrement, transfer to $L$ & 32\\\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Event counts include all transfer crossings and bounces. The nondestructive test already counts its forward/inverse interface once.}\label{smc:br:tab:compile}
\end{table}

Every marker-only rule has an instruction-specific moving-marker input, and the inverse marker labels are branch tagged. Thus different contexts do not force conflicting outputs on the same input. No collision changes a label at a distance. The explicit rules either have distinct inputs or agree on their prescribed output; fresh phase copies ensure distinctness whenever contexts differ.

\subsection{Completion of the finite table}
Complete the table by identity rules on every otherwise unspecified finite label set with pairwise distinct speeds. The alphabet is finite, so this completion is finite and deterministic. It preserves cardinality. The complete chronology proofs ensure that these default rules insert no extra event along an encoded execution: there is no additional meeting at which one would be used.

A single common speed set for every compiled program is
\begin{equation}\label{smc:br:eq:speeds}
 \{0\}\ \cup\ \pm\left\{1,\frac13,\frac1{79},\frac1{41},\frac32,\frac14,4,\frac12,2\right\}.
\end{equation}
Its nine positive magnitudes, their negatives and zero give 19 speeds. Forward testing, reverse testing and reflection account for the signs; the update speeds are \eqref{smc:br:eq:updatespeeds}. The number of finite labels depends on the program, but these 19 speed values do not. This is an upper bound, not an optimization result.

\subsection{Inductive simulation proof}
The initial section satisfies \eqref{smc:br:eq:encoding}. At each nonhalting instruction, Section~\ref{smc:br:sec:encoding} selects the correct zero or positive chamber for every encoded counter pair. The test restores the same coordinates. Section~\ref{smc:br:sec:updates} implements precisely the instructed update, with every intermediate guard valid. The block interfaces restore the standard section and emit exactly the correct next control label. Induction on instruction count proves correctness for every finite computation prefix and hence for any unbounded run.

For rational $D$, every initial position is rational and every finite event time and collision position is rational: all speeds and all displayed affine formulas are rational. The theorem also permits real positive scale as a geometric rescaling; it makes no arbitrary-real-input universality claim.

\subsection{Uniform time and the no-accumulation conclusion}
Equations~\eqref{smc:br:eq:testtimes} and \eqref{smc:br:eq:bands} imply
\[
 D<T_{A\text{-test}}<4D.
\]
For the zero branch this follows from $x=3D/20$ and $17D/20\le y<19D/20$. For the positive branch, $D/20<x\le D/10$ gives $25D/18<T<25D/9$. \wtag\ (The upper bound is attained at $a=1$; read $\le$. See Remark~\ref{smc:xii:rem:atest}.) Adding two transfers gives $3D<T_{B\text{-test with transfers}}<6D$. Updates have duration strictly between $2D$ and $4D$, and each transfer takes exactly $D$. Therefore every nonhalting instruction satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{smc:br:eq:instructiontime}
 D<T_{\mathrm{instruction}}<10D.
\end{equation}
The largest block count in Table~\ref{smc:br:tab:compile} is 32.

Before halt every position remains in $[0,D]$: the changing-test tables and reflected inverse do; an update's moving target stays between its anchor and spectator; transfers traverse only that interval. The scale $D$ never changes. If $s_n$ is the time of the $n$th completed instruction, then $s_n>nD$ for $n>0$. Thus any bounded time interval contains only finitely many instructions, each having finitely many positively separated events. An infinite encoded computation has no finite-time collision accumulation, including no accumulation hidden inside an instruction. No post-accumulation continuation is used.

\subsection{What halting means}
The principal convention is reachability of the full section with a designated control label $Q_H$. This is a precise observable section event, not a claim that all five physical strands stop moving.

A finite-collision convention is also available: assign $Q_H$ speed $+1$ and identity crossings with $X,Y,R$. The messenger then leaves to the right, with exactly three subsequent crossings and no later collision. The four markers remain, so the live population is still five. Spatial confinement after that halt is not claimed. A separately specified harmless bounce cycle could retain confinement, but then finite-collision halting would no longer be the convention. These alternatives are distinct and must not be silently combined.
\section{A quartic certificate for a fixed instruction horizon}\label{smc:br:sec:certificate}
This arithmetic result is independent of the physical implementation. Its final corollary transports a native finite-trace certificate through Theorem~\ref{smc:br:thm:compiler}. The horizon indexes a family of polynomials with growing witness arity; it is not an additional input to one fixed-arity polynomial.

\subsection{Fixed transition data and positive inputs}
Fix a deterministic two-counter program $M$, an initial control state $q_0$ and one designated halt state $H$. Assign distinct integer codes to the states. Split each conditional into a zero edge and a positive-decrement edge, and add exactly one absorbing halt edge $h$. This edge is \emph{virtual padding} of a terminated native trace. It does not describe the post-halt motion of the physical escape convention.

Let the $E$ edges have fixed data
\[
 (u_e,v_e,d_e,f_e),\qquad e=1,\ldots,E,
\]
where $u_e,v_e$ are source/target state codes, and $d_e,f_e\in\{-1,0,1\}$ are the counter changes. An increment state has one edge. A conditional has exactly two edges: its zero edge has both changes zero and a zero guard on the tested counter; its positive edge decrements that counter. The halt edge has $u_h=v_h=H$ and $d_h=f_h=0$. Even if conditional targets coincide, the two guarded edges remain distinct. Duplicate copies of an enabled edge are not allowed, since witnesses identify individual edges.

Let $E_{A0}$ and $E_{B0}$ be the zero-edge sets, and put $Z=|E_{A0}|+|E_{B0}|$. If $I$ and $C$ count increment and conditional states, excluding the halt state, then
\begin{equation}\label{smc:br:eq:edgecounts}
 E=I+2C+1,\qquad Z=C.
\end{equation}
The native input counters are $a=A-1$, $b=B-1$, where $A,B$ are positive integers.

\begin{theorem}[Unique bounded-horizon witness]\label{smc:br:thm:quartic}
For each fixed $T\ge1$ there is an explicit integer polynomial
\[
 P_{M,T}(A,B;W)
\]
of total degree exactly four, including its two native input variables, such that $P_{M,T}=0$ has a positive-integer witness if and only if $M$ reaches $H$ within $T$ transitions from $(q_0,A-1,B-1)$. Whenever a witness exists it is unique. The construction has exactly
\begin{align}
 &T(E+2) &&\text{positive witness variables},\label{smc:br:eq:ledger}\\
 &T(E+Z+4)+1 &&\text{residual equations before bundling},\nonumber\\
 &1 &&\text{final polynomial equation}.\nonumber
\end{align}
A first-halt-exactly-$T$ variant has the same witnesses and degree, with one additional residual. The $T=0$ case is constant and is treated separately below.
\end{theorem}
\wtag\ [The device---one-hot step selectors, affine counter updates, positivity of the next shifted counter as the decrement guard, a sum of squares with a unique witness, and arity growing with the horizon---is that of Part~V's Theorem~\ref{smc:tm:thm:certificate} and Part~III's Theorem~\ref{smc:cs:thm:packet}; the object, a two-counter program with native shifted counters, is new here. In this section $E$ and $Z$ are counts, not sets, and $C$ counts conditional states (Equation~\eqref{smc:br:eq:edgecounts}); source~35 writes the same count~$J$. Part~XIII replaces the $T(E+2)$ witnesses by three, at a degree that grows with the horizon (Theorem~\ref{smc:bc:thm:main}).]

\subsection{Every witness and residual explicitly}
For $t=0,\ldots,T-1$ and $e=1,\ldots,E$, introduce a positive integer $w_{t,e}$ and abbreviate
\[
 s_{t,e}=w_{t,e}-1.
\]
For $t=1,\ldots,T$, introduce positive integer witnesses $A_t,B_t$. Set $A_0=A$, $B_0=B$ as abbreviations for the inputs, not new witnesses. There are $TE+2T$ witnesses in total.

The selector and one-hot residuals are
\begin{align}
 S_{t,e}&=(w_{t,e}-1)(w_{t,e}-2),&&0\le t<T,\quad1\le e\le E,\label{smc:br:eq:selector}\\
 O_t&=\sum_e s_{t,e}-1,&&0\le t<T.\label{smc:br:eq:onehot}
\end{align}
Vanishing forces $w_{t,e}\in\{1,2\}$, hence $s_{t,e}\in\{0,1\}$, with exactly one selected edge per step. Inactive selectors are uniquely $w=1$; they introduce no free padding values.

The exact counter-update residuals are affine:
\begin{align}
 U_t&=A_{t+1}-A_t-\sum_e d_e s_{t,e},\label{smc:br:eq:counterresidual}\\
 V_t&=B_{t+1}-B_t-\sum_e f_e s_{t,e},\qquad0\le t<T.\nonumber
\end{align}
If the selected edge decrements $A$, then $A_{t+1}=A_t-1>0$, so $A_t\ge2$. Thus the native entering counter is positive. The next-counter positivity already implements the positive-decrement guard, with no extra residual or witness. The same applies to $B$. One-hot selection is essential; it prevents sums of displacements from disguising an invalid decrement.

For every step and each zero edge include
\begin{equation}\label{smc:br:eq:zeroresidual}
 Z_{t,e}=\begin{cases}
 s_{t,e}(A_t-1),&e\in E_{A0},\\
 s_{t,e}(B_t-1),&e\in E_{B0}.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
A selected zero edge forces the native counter to vanish. An inactive zero edge contributes the zero residual without constraining that counter.

Finally include control residuals
\begin{align}
 C_{\mathrm{initial}}&=\sum_e u_e s_{0,e}-q_0,\label{smc:br:eq:controlresidual}\\
 C_t&=\sum_e v_e s_{t,e}-\sum_e u_e s_{t+1,e},&&0\le t<T-1,\nonumber\\
 C_{\mathrm{final}}&=\sum_e v_e s_{T-1,e}-H.\nonumber
\end{align}
There are $1+(T-1)+1=T+1$ such equations, also when $T=1$. Distinct state codes and one-hot selection ensure these compare actual states, not weighted averages of codes. State codes are fixed coefficients, not additional witnesses.

\subsection{Correctness and uniqueness}
Suppose the native computation first reaches $H$ after $k\le T$ transitions. Follow its unique edge sequence for $k$ steps and the unique halt loop for the remaining $T-k$ steps. Set each selected edge's $w$ to 2, every other $w$ to 1, and $A_t,B_t$ to the native counter values after $t$ padded steps, plus one. All are positive. Each displayed residual vanishes. If $k=0$, the whole padded sequence consists of halt edges.

Conversely, vanishing selectors and one-hot equations determine a single edge $e_t$ at every step. The control residuals start its path at $q_0$, join consecutive source and target states, and end it at $H$. The counter equations implement exactly that path's updates. A selected zero edge is valid by \eqref{smc:br:eq:zeroresidual}; a selected decrement is valid by positivity of the next shifted counter. Increment and halt edges are unconditionally valid. Hence the witnesses define a genuine padded native computation, and deleting its halt-loop suffix gives a first halt no later than $T$.

At an increment state one edge is possible. At a conditional with shifted tested counter 1, the zero edge is valid and a decrement would make the next shifted counter zero. At shifted counter at least 2, the zero edge is impossible and exactly the decrement edge is valid. At $H$ there is one padding edge. Induction from the fixed input therefore fixes every edge and next counter pair uniquely. It then fixes every $w$ uniquely to 1 or 2. This proves uniqueness of the entire positive witness tuple, including the inactive selectors.

\subsection{One polynomial, exact degree and exact counts}
Let $\mathcal R$ be the explicitly displayed list of residuals \eqref{smc:br:eq:selector}--\eqref{smc:br:eq:controlresidual}, and define
\begin{equation}\label{smc:br:eq:SOS}
 P_{M,T}=\sum_{r\in\mathcal R}r^2.
\end{equation}
This specifies the integer polynomial without needing a monomial expansion. A sum of squares of integers is zero exactly when all residuals are zero.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.2}
\begin{tabular}{@{}l c @{\hspace{2em}} c@{}}\toprule
Residual group & Count & Degree before squaring\\\midrule
Selectors & $TE$ & 2\\
One-hot selection & $T$ & 1\\
Two counter updates & $2T$ & 1\\
Zero guards & $TZ$ & 2\\
Initial, linking, final control & $T+1$ & 1\\\midrule
Total & $T(E+Z+4)+1$ & at most 2\\\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Exact ledger for the displayed positive-$T$ construction. Counts refer to displayed equation slots, including redundant or identically zero residuals for degenerate programs or state codes. They are not irredundancy, rank or minimality bounds.}\label{smc:br:tab:certificate}
\end{table}
The total degree is at most four, jointly in inputs and witnesses. It is exactly four: $E\ge1$ because the halt edge exists, and every squared selector residual contributes $w_{t,e}^4$ with coefficient 1. Other residuals are at most linear in that selector, so their squares cannot cancel its pure fourth power. This proves Theorem~\ref{smc:br:thm:quartic}.

There are no state witnesses, sign witnesses, unconstrained padding witnesses or hidden existential bounds. In instruction counts, \eqref{smc:br:eq:edgecounts} gives
\begin{align}
 \#W&=T(I+2C+3),\label{smc:br:eq:instructionledger}\\
 \#\mathcal R&=T(I+3C+5)+1,\nonumber\\
 \#\text{variables including inputs}&=2+T(I+2C+3).\nonumber
\end{align}

\subsection{Exact first halt, zero horizon and the family boundary}
For first halt exactly at $T\ge1$, add the single linear residual
\begin{equation}\label{smc:br:eq:earlyhalt}
 H_{\mathrm{early}}=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}s_{t,h}.
\end{equation}
Every selector is nonnegative, so $H_{\mathrm{early}}=0$ forbids any padded halt edge before final arrival. With $C_{\mathrm{final}}=0$, the first arrival at $H$ must then be the $T$th transition. Conversely every such trace satisfies \eqref{smc:br:eq:earlyhalt}. Thus
\[
 P^{\mathrm{exact}}_{M,T}=P_{M,T}+H_{\mathrm{early}}^2
\]
has the same unique witness property, degree four and $T(E+2)$ witnesses, with $T(E+Z+4)+2$ residuals. If $q_0=H$ and $T\ge1$, the by-horizon form has its unique all-loop witness, while the exact-first-halt form has none.

For $T=0$ use the constant polynomial
\begin{equation}\label{smc:br:eq:horizonzero}
 P_{M,0}=(q_0-H)^2.
\end{equation}
There are zero witnesses. The empty tuple is a solution precisely when the initial control state is already $H$, also the first-halt-at-zero condition. The positive-horizon quartic claim and ledger do not apply.

For fixed $M$, these are effectively specified polynomials indexed by $T$. Their arity grows with $T$. It is true that the native program halts if and only if \emph{some member} of the family has a witness. This does not create one fixed-arity Diophantine representation of unbounded halting, nor a finite-fold or single-fold result for such a representation. A packing construction would need to encode and verify a variable-length trace with finitely many integers and account for its own arithmetic modules. No packing, exponentiation, Pell or MRDP module is assumed here. \wtag\ [Source~35 (Section~\ref{smc:ck:sec:power}) adds two Pell POWER modules that pay for the exponential initialization inside the polynomial (the gaps themselves still have numeric height $\Theta(2^m)$, Theorem~\ref{smc:ck:thm:primitive}), not to pack the trace, and Part~XIII bounds the number of witnesses at each horizon; neither gives one fixed-arity representation of unbounded halting.]

\subsection{Transport to physical instruction sections}
For positive input $A,B$ initialize the fixed physical compiler by
\begin{equation}\label{smc:br:eq:physicalcertificateinput}
 x=D\left(\frac1{20}+\frac1{10}2^{-(A-1)}\right),\qquad
 y=D\left(\frac{19}{20}-\frac1{10}2^{-(B-1)}\right).
\end{equation}
This exponential initialization is separate from the polynomial. Its powers are not concealed polynomial terms or witness constraints. Positive rational $D$ gives rational initial coordinates.

Theorem~\ref{smc:br:thm:compiler} now implies that $P_{M,T}=0$ has its unique positive witness exactly when this encoded physical run reaches the designated halt section within $T$ simulated native instructions. The exact variant characterizes first arrival at the $T$th instruction section. Only the physical prefix ending at first halt is used; the virtual padding edge is never asserted to be physically executed.

If first halt occurs at $k>0$, elapsed time lies strictly between $kD$ and $10kD$, with at most $32k$ binary events. If $k=0$, the initial section already carries the halt label. An instruction horizon is not a fixed collision count, because instruction branches have different event counts. This transport is a bounded native reachability statement through a proved encoding; it is not a polynomial predicate on arbitrary real or rational physical coordinates.
\section{Interpretation and further questions}\label{smc:br:sec:scope}
\subsection{What the construction establishes}
The local changing-test maps are nontrivial affine maps of the homogeneous section data; their physical inverse erases that coordinate change while preserving the finite branch phase. This resolves the data-restoration problem at the level of complete configurations, not just one coordinate. The separated encoding then resolves a different problem: both counters can be updated forever with the same finite rule table, because every encoded state satisfies every needed guard.

The proof uses exact rational geometry and discrete instruction semantics. It is not a physical finite-precision implementation, a noise-robust coding theorem, a proof of minimum population or speed count, a globally reversible completion, or an optimal collision compiler. The five-live-signal count is a prior computational precedent \cite{dl2004mcu}; the inverse principle is also standard \cite{DL06}. The finite-label/live-occurrence distinction follows the usual model terminology \cite{agc10}. Any discrete universality corollary must use the precise instruction semantics, a point emphasized in the counter-machine literature \cite{dudenhefner2022}.

\subsection{Questions left open by this proof}
\begin{enumerate}
 \item \textbf{Can the same full-section interface use fewer speeds?}
 The set in \eqref{smc:br:eq:speeds} is chosen for explicit rational arithmetic, not minimality. It is open here whether forward/reverse test phases and both update signs can share a smaller speed alphabet without losing deterministic binary chronology. \wtag\ (Open. Source~35's clock adds ten speed magnitudes, Equation~\eqref{smc:ck:eq:addspeeds}, and asks the same question for its 39 speeds.)
 \item \textbf{Can the test avoid undoing its whole geometry?}
 The current nondestructive primitive pays for a complete physical inverse. A direct data-restoring branch might reduce the 14/12 event counts while keeping both exact chambers and literal stationary-label restoration.
 \item \textbf{Can all instruction transitions have one constant duration?}
 The present uniform bounds suffice for no accumulation, but the duration still depends on the encoded shape and branch. An exact constant-time padding block must itself preserve the same full section and use no additional live strand; no such construction is supplied. \wtag\ (Added 4 October 2026: answered for this compiler by source~35, Theorem~\ref{smc:ck:thm:clock}. Identity shuttles of the messenger between the four unmoved markers make every instruction last exactly $30D$, at the cost of 39 speeds and at most 54 contacts; smaller clocks stay open, Section~\ref{smc:ck:sec:future}.)
 \item \textbf{Can a completed table be globally reversible?}
 Fresh inverse phases make each selected return invertible as a gadget. Global reversibility of a total finite collision table is a stronger compatibility problem, especially where distinct control paths merge. It is not resolved by adding identity rules. \wtag\ (Open. Part~III's machine is globally reversible, but it is a different, universal construction with 18 live signals.)
 \item \textbf{What quantitative precision is needed for a finite computation?}
 The guard margins for branching are uniform, yet adjacent counter values converge geometrically. A useful finite-horizon perturbation analysis would separately quantify branch safety, counter distinguishability and accumulated timing error; no robustness statement follows just from the margins.
 \item \textbf{How should collision and label complexity trade off?}
 Instruction-specific copying makes deterministic compilation transparent. A smaller finite control alphabet might reuse phases, but only after proving that marker-only rules and returning messengers cannot become ambiguous. No optimality result is known from this argument.
\end{enumerate}
A separate arithmetic question is whether a rigorously costed packing mechanism can replace the growing-arity horizon family by a fixed-arity representation while retaining useful degree or witness bounds. The unique witnesses proved for each horizon alone do not answer it. \wtag\ (Open as posed. Part~XIII reduces the witnesses at each horizon to a bounded number---Theorems~\ref{smc:bc:thm:gapmain}, \ref{smc:pp:thm:maincomposition} and~\ref{smc:la:thm:composition}---but its polynomials are still indexed by the horizon.)

These questions concern stronger properties than the theorems proved here. They are not claims that the properties are impossible.

The README gives the commands.] The arithmetic audit independently verifies the residual schema, quartic coefficients, guards and finite-polynomial candidate words. Its finite checks support, but do not replace, the general proof of positive-witness correctness and uniqueness.

No author scientific program, upstream constructor, native counter interpreter, physical simulator, saved physical collision schedule or proof-assistant program was executed during manuscript preparation. Scientific source files are inert preserved evidence. \wtag\ [The placement ran them only on throw-away copies; their outputs agree with the recorded evidence up to checker self-hashes, line endings and path separators.] The diagram substitutes exact rational coordinates into the proved formulas; it is not generated by a collision scheduler.

\subsection{Release and review records}
The archive contains the editable LaTeX modules and their deterministic standalone flattening, final PDF, scientific sources, independent audit dossiers and release-only tools. Its README gives review outcomes and portable replay commands. Mathematical audit, manuscript transcription checks and integrity checks are distinct; their overlapping counts are not additive theorem counts.

The typesetting build uses a fresh TeX format with no shell escape and records the dependency union from every pass. A locked rebuild authenticates external manuscript and toolchain pins, checks packaged PDF equality, and renders and validates every page. The dependency lock covers executable bytes and recorded system inputs, not shared libraries, Python's standard library or the operating system. The deterministic archive and its extractor preserve manifest-bound file and directory metadata.

Independent tool review and all-page manuscript review bind the exact final versions identified in the README and external handoff. All original scientific bytes, modes and nanosecond mtimes are preserved. A final independent terminal audit precedes publication. \wtag\ (No record of it is in the archive; see Section~\ref{smc:xii:sec:further}, item~\ref{smc:xii:q:terminal}.)

\begin{quote}\small
We add two explicit refinements to the five-live-signal counter compiler of Report~64 [source~34]. First, stationary identity shuttles pad each instruction to exactly $30D$ time, where $D$ is the preserved anchor distance. The same five signals suffice; at most 54 binary contacts occur per instruction, including identity crossings, and one common set of 39 rational speeds works for every finite source program. A general output-linear padding lemma implements every phase change at a real contact. Second, a bounded-halting polynomial accepts three native positive integer gaps, paying for their exponential decoding inside two fully displayed 15-residual POWER modules. For a fixed program and horizon $T$, the formula has exactly $T(E+2)+54$ positive witnesses, $T(E+Z+4)+33$ residuals, and joint degree 12. Here $E$ includes split conditional edges and one virtual halt loop, while $Z$ counts zero edges. Accepted gaps decode uniquely and determine a unique padded trace, but every nonempty full witness fiber is infinite. We also derive the exact primitive integer initialization, its gcd and minimum scale, and its bit-height cost. The predicate includes being encoded, and the horizon indexes a growing-arity family. Neither arbitrary unencoded physical halting nor a fixed-arity unbounded-halting representation is claimed. Five-signal computation and bouncing delays have prior precedents; no priority or optimality claim is made.
\end{quote}
\section{Results and their precise scope}\label{smc:ck:sec:main}
A finite signal-machine label has one fixed rational speed. A live signal is an occurrence of a label. Our population count is five live signals, regardless of how many finite phase labels a program needs. At an instruction section the four stationary markers and the outgoing messenger are
\begin{equation}\label{smc:ck:eq:section}
L=0,\quad X=x,\quad Y=y,\quad R=D,\qquad
Q_i\text{ at }L\text{ with speed }+1,\qquad 0<x<y<D.
\end{equation}
The literal stationary labels are $L,X_0,Y,R$. The two outgoing strands at $L$ are counted separately. An instruction is a transition from a nonhalting control state; its destination may be the halt state. All contacts used below are binary, with distinct incoming and outgoing speeds. Identity crossings count as contacts.

\begin{theorem}[Exactly clocked compiler]\label{smc:ck:thm:clock}
For each fixed finite deterministic two-counter program with increments, zero-test/positive-decrement instructions and a designated halt state, there is a finite rational-speed collision table which simulates every pair $(a,b)\in\NN^2$ from the encoding
\begin{equation}\label{smc:ck:eq:encoding}
x=D\left(\frac1{20}+\frac1{10}2^{-a}\right),\qquad
y=D\left(\frac{19}{20}-\frac1{10}2^{-b}\right),\qquad D>0.
\end{equation}
Each instruction takes exactly $30D$, uses at most 54 contacts, and restores the full section with the prescribed new counters and next control label. Exactly five signals remain live. A single set of 39 rational speeds suffices for all finite programs. First halt after $k$ instructions occurs at exactly $30kD$ and after at most $54k$ contacts. An infinite computation has no finite-time collision accumulation.
\end{theorem}

The clock is constant across counter values, branches and instructions within each run. It scales with the unchanged $D$; it is 30 in normalized units $D=1$. The finite label and rule counts can depend on the program. No instruction is performed at the halt state. Three optional post-halt escape crossings are separate from the $54k$ prefix bound and do not change the first-halt time.

For the arithmetic theorem, fix integer codes for the program states, initial state $q_0$ and halt state $H$. Split each conditional into a zero edge and a decrement edge, and add one virtual absorbing edge at $H$. Let $E$ be the total number of edges and $Z$ the number of zero edges. If there are $I$ increment instructions and $J$ conditional instructions, then $E=I+2J+1$ and $Z=J$. \wtag\ [Source~34 writes this count~$C$ (Equation~\eqref{smc:br:eq:edgecounts}). Here $J$ and $Z$ are counts, unrelated to the Pell leaves $J_A,J_B$ of Section~\ref{smc:ck:sec:power} and to the integers~$\Z$.]

\begin{definition}[Native encoded halting]\label{smc:ck:def:native}
For external inputs $(g_1,g_2,g_3)\in\Np^3$, set
\begin{equation}\label{smc:ck:eq:gaps}
D=g_1+g_2+g_3,\qquad x=g_1,\qquad y=g_1+g_2.
\end{equation}
A triple is encoded when there are $a,b\in\NN$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{smc:ck:eq:nativeencoding}
\frac{g_1}{D}=\frac1{20}+\frac1{10}2^{-a},\qquad
\frac{g_3}{D}=\frac1{20}+\frac1{10}2^{-b}.
\end{equation}
For a fixed integer $T\geq0$, $\EncHalt_{M,T}(g)$ means that $g$ is encoded and its decoded computation reaches $H$ in at most $T$ instructions.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Native positive gap certificate]\label{smc:ck:thm:native}
The explicit integer polynomial $F_{M,T}$ in Section~\ref{smc:ck:sec:polynomial} satisfies
\[
\EncHalt_{M,T}(g_1,g_2,g_3)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists W\in\Np^{\,T(E+2)+54}\;F_{M,T}(g;W)=0.
\]
It has three external inputs, exactly $T(E+Z+4)+33$ residual equations before sum-of-squares bundling, and joint total degree exactly 12. The counts include $T=0$. For $T\geq1$, first halt exactly at $T$ requires one additional residual, no additional witnesses and no degree increase. Decoded counters and the trace projection are unique, but each accepted input has infinitely many full witnesses.
\end{theorem}

The three external inputs are unrestricted positive integers; the \emph{predicate itself} includes encoding. An unencoded triple has no witness, independently of any physical behavior outside the encoded simulation. $D$ is the expression in \eqref{smc:ck:eq:gaps}, not another input. There is no externally supplied exponential initialization. The horizon fixes the number of variables and residuals: this is a growing-arity family, not one fixed-arity polynomial with a free unbounded time variable.

\section{The inherited core and its output coordinate costs}\label{smc:ck:sec:core}
Report~64 [source~34] proves a single fixed-ordered-section compiler with uniform guards on \eqref{smc:ck:eq:encoding}. Its core trajectories, all-input guard proof, literal marker restoration and finite-rule construction are retained unchanged as an explicit dependency. We summarize exactly what is used, then derive the new elapsed-time expressions independently. \wtag\ [The statements summarized in this subsection are source~34's: the scaling and translation guards \eqref{smc:br:eq:scaleguard} and~\eqref{smc:br:eq:translationguard}, the updates \eqref{smc:br:eq:increment} and~\eqref{smc:br:eq:decrement}, the test chambers and durations (Theorem~\ref{smc:br:thm:test} and Equation~\eqref{smc:br:eq:testtimes}), the encoding margins \eqref{smc:br:eq:zero-margins} and~\eqref{smc:br:eq:positive-margins}, and the transfers of Section~\ref{smc:br:sec:encoding}.]

\subsection{Core operations and uniform guards}
In nearest-target coordinates let $t$ be the target distance, $s$ the spectator distance and $D$ the far anchor distance. The inherited four-contact scaling $t\mapsto kt$ has guard
\[
0<t<s<D,\qquad 0<kt<s,
\]
duration $2(1+k)t$, and moving-target speed $(k-1)/(k+1)$. The ten-contact translation $t\mapsto t+eD$ for $e<1$ has guard
\[
0<t<s<D,\qquad 0<t+eD<s,
\]
and duration $2[t+t/(1-e)]+2D$. Its intermediate target $t/(1-e)$ lies between $t$ and $t+eD$. Each operation restores its anchor section and all stationary labels. Every spectator crossing is included in its count.

For $t=D/20+(D/10)2^{-n}$, increment is
\[
t\longmapsto t/2\longmapsto t/2+D/40,
\]
using $k=1/2,e=1/40$. Positive decrement is
\[
t\longmapsto 2t\longmapsto 2t-D/20,
\]
using $k=2,e=-1/20$. For all $n\geq0$, $D/20<t\leq3D/20$. On a positive decrement $n\geq1$ gives $t\leq D/10$, so even the doubled intermediate target is at most $D/5<s$, since $s\geq17D/20$. These inequalities guard all endpoints and hidden translation stages.

The inherited nondestructive A test restores its input section with branch-specific outgoing labels. Its zero word has 14 contacts and duration $25(2x+y)/9$, with exact chamber $4x<y<8x$ inside the ordered section. Its positive word has 12 contacts and duration $250x/9$, with exact chamber $8x<y$. If $a=0$, then $x=3D/20$ and $17D/20\leq y<19D/20$, which lies in the zero chamber. If $a>0$, $x\leq D/10$, whence $y-8x\geq D/20>0$. Thus all encoded states satisfy the appropriate strict guard. The B operation reflects the construction in $R$, using target $D-y$, spectator $D-x$, and two unit-speed transfers with three contacts each.

This report does not replace the core's chronology proof by a timing identity. The complete frozen core proof, including the changing test, its physically implemented inverse and all primitive rules, accompanies the release. \wtag\ [It is source~34's physical packet, shipped once as \path{34-branching-science-frozen-proof-PROOF.md}; its arguments are printed in Sections~\ref{smc:br:sec:branch}--\ref{smc:br:sec:compiler}.] The newly proved padding below has the larger guard $0<x<y<D$.

\subsection{Elapsed time in the available output geometry}
Let $(D,x',y')$ be the section \emph{after} a core completes. Padding sees these values. We need
\begin{equation}\label{smc:ck:eq:corelinear}
T_c=\alpha_cD+\beta_cx'+\gamma_cy'.
\end{equation}
The complete coefficient ledger is Table~\ref{smc:ck:tab:coretime}.

Branch & $\alpha_c$ & $\beta_c$ & $\gamma_c$ & Core contacts\\\midrule
A increment & $341/195$ & $392/39$ & $0$ & 14\\
A zero & $0$ & $50/9$ & $25/9$ & 14\\
A positive & $383/126$ & $1310/63$ & $0$ & 26\\
B increment & $69/5$ & $0$ & $-392/39$ & 20\\

\end{table}
The nearest-target update durations are
\begin{align}
T_{\rm inc}(t)&=3t+2\left[\frac t2+\frac{t/2}{1-1/40}\right]+2D
=2D+\frac{196}{39}t,\label{smc:ck:eq:incduration}\\
T_{\rm dec}(t)&=6t+2\left[2t+\frac{2t}{1+1/20}\right]+2D
=2D+\frac{290}{21}t.\label{smc:ck:n7}
\end{align}
Adding the positive-test time gives
\begin{equation}\label{smc:ck:eq:posduration}
T_{\rm pos}(t)=\frac{250}{9}t+T_{\rm dec}(t)
=2D+\frac{2620}{63}t.
\end{equation}
For A increment, $x'=t/2+D/40$, hence $t=2x'-D/20$; substitution gives the first row. For A positive, $x'=2t-D/20$, hence $t=x'/2+D/40$; substitution gives the third. The nondestructive zero time is already $25(2x'+y')/9$.

For B write $r$ for the old distance to the B target from $R$. Two transfers add $2D$. Increment gives
\[
r=2(D-y')-D/20=39D/20-2y',\qquad
T=4D+(196/39)r=(69/5)D-(392/39)y'.
\]
Positive decrement gives
\[
r=(D-y')/2+D/40=21D/40-y'/2,\qquad
T=4D+(2620/63)r=(155/6)D-(1310/63)y'.
\]
The reflected zero test yields
\[
T=2D+\frac{25}{9}\bigl[2(D-y')+(D-x')\bigr]
=\frac{31}{3}D-\frac{25}{9}x'-\frac{50}{9}y'.
\]
These identities hold on the admitted domain of the respective core. They do not assert that every branch is meaningful on every ordered section.

\section{Stationary shuttles and a general clock padding lemma}\label{smc:ck:sec:padding}
Drop primes temporarily and let $a_0=x$, $b_0=y-x$, $c_0=D-y$. All three are strictly positive. The four markers stay at their literal labels and positions throughout padding. Only the messenger moves. For a fixed positive rational $v$, every listed flight has duration equal to its length divided by $v$.

\caption{Complete padding words. Departure is not a new contact; the terminal contact is included. All identity crossings are counted.}\label{smc:ck:tab:shuttles}

\subsection{Every phase change occurs at a contact}
Give every occurrence of every primitive fresh messenger labels, tagged by instruction, branch and stage. Let $S$ be an anchor, $U$ its chosen target, and $B_0$ any intervening marker. A round trip has an outward label $p_{\rm out}$ of speed $\varepsilon v$ and inward label $p_{\rm in}$ of speed $-\varepsilon v$, where $\varepsilon=1$ from $L$ and $-1$ from $R$. Its rules are
\begin{align}
\{p_{\rm out},U\}&\ruleto\{p_{\rm in},U\},&
\{p_{\rm in},S\}&\ruleto\{q_{\rm next},S\},\label{smc:ck:eq:looprule}\\
\{p_{\rm out},B_0\}&\ruleto\{p_{\rm out},B_0\},&
\{p_{\rm in},B_0\}&\ruleto\{p_{\rm in},B_0\}.\label{smc:ck:n10}
\end{align}
The label $q_{\rm next}$ has the already specified speed of the next primitive. For the full-span loop $S=L,U=R$ and both $X,Y$ are intervening markers. A transfer label $p_{\rm tr}$ has speed $+1$ or $-1$, identity crossings at $X,Y$, and destination rule
\begin{equation}\label{smc:ck:eq:transferrule}
\{p_{\rm tr},U\}\ruleto\{q_{\rm next},U\}.
\end{equation}
There is no separate departure rule. The preceding terminal contact emits the next departure label. All inputs and outputs consist of one speed-zero marker and a nonzero-speed messenger. Fresh occurrence labels prevent conflicting input rules. Unused finite distinct-speed inputs may receive cardinality-preserving identity rules as in the core.

\subsection{Exact chronology on the whole ordered section}
Every flight in Table~\ref{smc:ck:tab:shuttles} crosses one open interval between consecutive stationary markers, with positive length $a_0$, $b_0$ or $c_0$. There is no other marker in its interior. At a crossing the messenger continues in the same direction; at a target it reverses; at a terminal anchor it leaves in the next specified direction. Consequently the next listed contact is the next physical contact. At a contact with $L,X,Y,R$, the respective distances to the other markers are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
L & a_0,\ a_0+b_0,\ a_0+b_0+c_0\\
X & a_0,\ b_0,\ b_0+c_0\\
Y & a_0+b_0,\ b_0,\ c_0\\
R & a_0+b_0+c_0,\ b_0+c_0,\ c_0
\end{array}
\]
and all are positive. There is only one moving signal, so neither a remote simultaneous contact nor a triple contact can occur. No extra marker or temporary marker phase is introduced. The common guard is precisely the ordered section: its boundary identifies stationary markers or collapses a mandatory full-span flight, violating the strict binary-section convention.

\begin{lemma}[Output-linear clock padding]\label{smc:ck:lem:padding}
Suppose finitely many implemented cores return to \eqref{smc:ck:eq:section} with an outgoing $+1$ messenger at $L$, and branch $c$ has time \eqref{smc:ck:eq:corelinear} in its output coordinates. If the rational constant $C>0$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{smc:ck:eq:Cbound}
C>4+\alpha_c+\max(\beta_c,0)+\max(\gamma_c,0)
\end{equation}
for every branch, each core admits five-live-signal identity padding to total time $CD$. Padding uses at most 26 contacts. For a finite core family its rational speeds and labels are finite and independent of the coordinates.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Fix a branch and put
\begin{align*}
\ell_X&=\max(-\beta,0),&r_X&=\max(\beta,0),\\
\ell_Y&=\max(-\gamma,0),&r_Y&=\max(\gamma,0),\\
k&=C-\alpha-r_X-r_Y-4>0.
\end{align*}
The required positive-distance decomposition is
\begin{equation}\label{smc:ck:eq:paddingtime}
CD-T_c=(4+k)D+\ell_Xx+\ell_Yy+r_X(D-x)+r_Y(D-y).
\end{equation}
Its coefficients are correct since $\ell_X-r_X=-\beta$, $\ell_Y-r_Y=-\gamma$, and $4+k+r_X+r_Y=C-\alpha$.

Execute the following order, omitting a target loop only when its coefficient is zero:
\begin{enumerate}
\item A unit-speed full $LRL$ loop, taking $2D$ and six contacts
\item $LXL$ at magnitude $2/\ell_X$, then $LYL$ at $2/\ell_Y$
\item The unit-speed $LR$ transfer, taking $D$ and three contacts
\item $RYR$ at magnitude $2/r_Y$, then $RXR$ at $2/r_X$
\item The unit-speed $RL$ transfer, taking $D$ and three contacts
\item A full $LRL$ loop at magnitude $2/k$, taking $kD$ and six contacts
\end{enumerate}
The first loop is essential: the inherited entry speed is $+1$. Its fresh terminal $L$ contact chooses the first different speed. The construction never silently replaces that outgoing speed at entry, and never inserts a zero-time extra event. Every later selection occurs at the terminal contact in \eqref{smc:ck:eq:looprule} or \eqref{smc:ck:eq:transferrule}. If a target loop is omitted, the preceding actual contact emits the next actual phase.

The fixed loops and transfers total $4D+kD$ and 18 contacts. At most one of $\ell_X,r_X$ and one of $\ell_Y,r_Y$ is nonzero. Thus at most two target loops occur, each with at most four contacts, giving at most 26. Their times add to \eqref{smc:ck:eq:paddingtime}. The positive-flight argument applies to every stage and at every interface; all coordinates and stationary labels are preserved. The final contact emits the next instruction's speed-$+1$ label.
\end{proof}
The bound \eqref{smc:ck:eq:Cbound} is sufficient, not necessary or optimal. Any finite rational output-linear family admits such a rational $C$. If the core templates are common to every program, the enlarged speed set is common too; only phase copies grow with program size.
